variants.label: Indian Complete Specification (Form 2)
variants.description: Complete specification for a patent application filed using Form 2 under the Patents Act, 1970 and Patents Rules, 2003.

ui.placeholder: Enter a concise technical title (≤15 words).
ui.helpText: Title must indicate the specific features of the invention and is normally in not more than 15 words, as per Rule 13(7)(a) of the Patents Rules, 2003. No strict character limit exists in the Rules; focus on brevity and clarity, avoiding trademarks, personal names and the word 'patent'.

ui.placeholder: State the technical field of the invention.
ui.helpText: 1–3 sentences indicating the technical field to which the invention relates; usually the opening part of the description as per the Manual of Patent Office Practice and Procedure.

ui.placeholder: Describe prior art and problems addressed by the invention.
ui.helpText: Briefly describe the prior art and the technical problem addressed. Avoid unnecessary admissions that specific documents are prior art and avoid statements implying the invention is obvious or a mere workshop modification.

ui.placeholder: State the principal and additional objects of the invention.
ui.helpText: Clearly articulate the technical problems associated with existing technology (prior art) and the specific solutions provided by the invention. Use statements like 'The principal object of this invention is to...' or 'Another object of this invention is to...' to outline specific goals achieved. This section should directly correlate with the features mentioned in the claims.

ui.placeholder: Provide a concise summary or statement of the invention.
ui.helpText: Provide a concise summary of the invention highlighting the essential features and distinguishing aspects over the known art, consistent with the independent claims. Recommended by the Manual to precede the detailed description for clarity.

ui.placeholder: List each figure briefly (e.g., 'FIG. 1 is a schematic view of ...').
ui.helpText: List each drawing figure with a one-line description (e.g., 'FIG. 1 is a schematic view of a system configuration'). Ensure figure numbering and captions match the drawing sheets filed under Rule 15.

ui.placeholder: Provide a full detailed description with reference to drawings where applicable.
ui.helpText: Describe the invention in full detail, including best mode, so that a person skilled in the art can perform the invention, as required by Section 10(4) of the Patents Act, 1970. Refer consistently to reference numerals in the drawings and provide sufficient embodiments to support all claims.

ui.placeholder: Write independent and dependent claims in separate numbered paragraphs.
ui.helpText: Claims must define the matter for which protection is sought and be supported by the description as per Section 10(4) and (5). Use clear, precise language; maintain unity of invention; and draft each claim as a single sentence with proper dependencies.

ui.placeholder: Short technical abstract (≤150 words) starting with the title.
ui.helpText: Provide a concise summary in not more than 150 words, commencing with the title of the invention and indicating the technical field, technical advancement and principal use of the invention, in line with Section 10(4)(d) and Rule 13(7)(b). Avoid claim-style wording.

drawings.colorUsageNote: Colour drawings are accepted only when absolutely essential for understanding; otherwise black-and-white line drawings in black ink are required under Rule 15.

procedural.gracePeriodNotes: India has no general grace period; only limited exceptions (e.g., Section 31 exhibitions and learned society disclosures) where specific conditions must be satisfied.

sequenceListing.lateFurnishingNotes: Sequence listing for nucleotide and amino acid sequences must be furnished in XML format compliant with WIPO Standard ST.26; text (TXT) or PDF may be filed for reference where permitted.

title.message: Title appears long; Indian practice under Rule 13(7)(a) expects a specific title normally in not more than 15 words.

abstract.message: Abstract exceeds the 150 word limit under Rule 13(7)(b).

claims.message: Number of claims exceeds 10; additional official fees apply for each claim beyond ten under the First Schedule. Keep claim set succinct and consistent with unity of invention under Section 10(5).

crossSectionChecks.message: Some claim elements may not be clearly supported in the detailed description as required by Section 10(4).
Abstract may describe features not clearly reflected in the independent claims; ensure consistency with the claimed subject-matter.

topUp.instruction: For Indian jurisdiction under Rule 13(7)(a), ensure the title is specific, indicates the features of the invention, and is normally expressed in not more than 15 words.
constraints: Avoid trademarks and personal names per Indian Patent Manual guidelines
Focus on brevity and clarity per Patents Rules, 2003

topUp.instruction: Per Indian Patent Office Manual of Practice and Procedure, this section opens the description and indicates the technical field to which the invention relates.
constraints: Limit to 1–3 sentences as per Manual guidelines
State the general and specific technical field without advantages or embodiments

topUp.instruction: Per Indian Patent Manual, briefly describe the prior art and the technical problem addressed. Exercise care in characterizing prior art to avoid prejudicing patentability.
constraints: Avoid unnecessary admissions that particular documents are prior art
Do not state that the invention is obvious, trivial or a mere workshop modification
Focus on technical limitations of conventional approaches

topUp.instruction: Per Indian Patent Office practice, draft the 'Object(s) of the Invention' section to clearly articulate the technical problems with existing prior art and the specific solutions provided by the invention. This section is placed after Background and before Summary in Indian Complete Specifications (Form 2).
constraints: Use statements beginning with 'The principal object of this invention is to...' or 'Another object of this invention is to...'
NEVER use 'The object...' (singular definite) as this implies only one objective
Focus on technical results achieved (e.g., 'to improve efficiency'), not the means
Each objective should correlate directly with features mentioned in the claims
Describe what the invention achieves, not how it achieves it
additions: Acknowledge closest prior art and clearly distinguish how the invention improves upon it
Ensure objectives can be substantiated by the detailed description and claims
Do not admit non-patentability or state invention is obvious
Avoid vague or non-technical goals focusing only on commercial success
Do not overstate benefits - stick to demonstrable technical advantages

topUp.instruction: Per Manual of Patent Office Practice and Procedure, provide a concise summary highlighting essential features and distinguishing aspects over known art, consistent with independent claims.
constraints: This summary should precede the detailed description for clarity
Ensure consistency with the scope of independent claims

topUp.instruction: Per Section 10(4) of the Patents Act, 1970, describe the invention in full detail including the best method of performing it, so that a person skilled in the art can work the invention.
constraints: Include best method of performing the invention as required by Section 10(4)(b)
Provide sufficient embodiments to support all claims
Refer consistently to reference numerals in drawings
additions: Each independent claim must have at least one supporting embodiment

topUp.instruction: Draft claims compliant with Section 10(4) and (5) of the Indian Patents Act, 1970. Claims must define the matter for which protection is sought, be clear and succinct, and be fairly based on the matter disclosed in the specification.
constraints: Use 'comprising' as preferred open connector; 'including' acceptable; 'consisting of' for narrow scope
Prefer two-part format (preamble + 'characterised in that') when defining improvements
Multiple dependent claims permitted including on other multiple dependent claims
Maintain unity of invention under Section 10(5)
additions: All claims must be fully supported by the detailed description
Each claim must define matter for which protection is sought per Section 10(4)

topUp.instruction: Per Section 10(4)(d) and Rule 13(7)(b), provide a concise summary in not more than 150 words, commencing with the title and indicating technical field, technical advancement, and principal use.
constraints: Hard limit of 150 words under Indian Rules
Must commence with the title of the invention
Indicate technical field, advancement, and principal use
additions: Avoid claim-style wording per Manual guidelines

topUp.instruction: List each drawing figure with a one-line description ensuring figure numbering and captions match the drawing sheets filed under Rule 15.
constraints: Use format: 'FIG. X is a [type] view of [subject]'
Ensure consistent numbering with actual drawing sheets

diagramGenerationHints.block: Use rectangles for components and arrows for data or control flow; keep labelling consistent with the detailed description.
diagramGenerationHints.flowchart: Use standard flowchart symbols for processes and decisions; ensure the flow reflects the claimed method steps.

checkList.description: Ensure all reference numerals in drawings are defined in the detailed description.
Ensure key claimed elements appear in at least one figure when drawings are present.

meta.office: Office of the Controller General of Patents, Designs & Trade Marks (CGPDTM)
meta.lawVersion: Patents Act 1970 + Patents Rules 2003 as amended by the Patents (Amendment) Rules 2024

deadlines.what: Reply to FER (application to be put in order for grant)

extension.note: 2024 Amendment Rules: the Form 4 request may be filed any time within 9 months of the FER date (Rule 24B(6)).

consequence.note: No statutory revival; only writ/appeal in rare procedural-failure cases.

deadlines.what: Updated Form 3 (Section 8 foreign-application details), if objected or due
deadlines.basis: Rule 12(3) as amended by the 2024 Rules

extension.note: Condonable up to 3 months on request (2024 Rules).

deadlines.what: Written submissions and relevant documents after hearing

consequence.note: Late written submissions may be disregarded; they also cannot introduce new arguments (DHC).

prosecution.note: FER → reply → (subsequent report or hearing u/s 14) → grant or refusal u/s 15. Quality of the FER reply usually decides whether prosecution ends in one round.

detectionHints: does not constitute an invention under section 2(1)(j)
objections.argumentSkeleton: For each cited document relied on for novelty: (1) identify the claim feature absent from that single document; (2) quote the exact passage the examiner relied on; (3) state the technical difference and its effect; (4) conclude that the document does not disclose all claimed features arranged as claimed.

caseLawWhitelist.name: Lallubhai Chakubhai Jariwala v. Chimanlal Chunilal
caseLawWhitelist.point: Anticipation requires a single prior disclosure containing the whole of the invention.

detectionHints: obvious to a person skilled in the art
objections.argumentSkeleton: Address the combination the examiner actually articulated: (1) what each cited document teaches on its own; (2) why the skilled person had no reason to combine them (or why the combination still misses a claim feature); (3) the technical advance or economic significance of the claimed feature over the closest art, tracking the words of s.2(1)(ja); (4) hindsight caution.

caseLawWhitelist.name: F. Hoffmann-La Roche Ltd v. Cipla Ltd
caseLawWhitelist.point: Obviousness must be assessed without hindsight, from the perspective of the person skilled in the art.

caseLawWhitelist.name: Avery Dennison Corp v. Controller of Patents
caseLawWhitelist.point: Even a small technical advance may support inventive step; examiner must give reasons for the combination.

detectionHints: falls within the scope of section 3

subTypes.guidance: CRI Guidelines 2025 (final, July 2025): demonstrate technical effect/technical contribution beyond the program per se; no novel-hardware requirement; anchor on how the claimed steps solve a technical problem (e.g. resource use, latency, reliability). Avoid arguing business advantage.

New form / new use / new property of a known substance needs enhanced known efficacy — for pharmaceuticals, therapeutic efficacy per Novartis v. Union of India; comparative data against the known substance is expected; bioavailability alone is insufficient. Examiners often pair 3(d) with an inventive-step objection.

Mere admixture / aggregation of known components: rebut by demonstrating a synergistic effect of the combination beyond the additive properties of the components, with data or worked examples in the specification.

Discovery of a living thing or non-living substance occurring in nature / mere discovery of a scientific principle: argue the claim is to a human-made product or a technical application, not the discovery itself.
Mere arrangement / re-arrangement of known devices each functioning independently: show functional interdependence producing a new combined result.
Methods of treatment/diagnosis of humans or animals are excluded — convert to product, composition, apparatus or in-vitro method claims.
Mere mental act / method of playing a game — show steps that necessarily involve technical means.

caseLawWhitelist.name: Novartis AG v. Union of India
caseLawWhitelist.point: Section 3(d) efficacy for pharmaceuticals means therapeutic efficacy.

caseLawWhitelist.name: Ferid Allani v. Union of India
caseLawWhitelist.point: Computer-implemented inventions with technical effect are not excluded by s.3(k).

objections.argumentSkeleton: Map each allegedly undisclosed element to the specification paragraph(s) and drawing(s) where it is described; where the objection targets best method, identify the embodiment disclosing it.

objections.localLabel: Claims not clear, concise or definitive
detectionHints: are not clearly and distinctly defined
do not sufficiently define the invention

subTypes.guidance: Clarity & conciseness: for each impugned/relative term give its meaning as the skilled person reads it in light of the specification (cite paragraphs), or amend to a precise, measurable formulation with basis.

Scope: examiner lists specific terms (e.g. 'ultrathin', 'lower frequencies') that are said to be overly broad / not defining the scope. Handle each listed term: add a structural/measurable limitation from the specification, or construe it definitely with a paragraph cite.

Definitiveness: often an antecedent-basis point ('a'/'an' for first use, 'the'/'said' thereafter) or functional/result-oriented language without structural limits. Fix antecedent basis by amendment; for functional language add objectively verifiable structural limitations from the specification.

objections.argumentSkeleton: Handle each impugned term individually: quote the examiner's specific term, then either (a) construe it definitely from the specification with a paragraph cite, or (b) amend to a precise/structural formulation and cite its basis. Indian FERs frequently split this into separate 'Clarity and Conciseness' and 'Definitiveness' objections — answer both if present.

Identify the shared special technical feature linking the claim groups; if election is unavoidable, elect the commercially central group and note the right to file a divisional under s.16 while the application is pending.
actions: Consider divisional application under Section 16 before grant if election is taken

detectionHints: particulars of applications filed outside India
objections.argumentSkeleton: Answer each disclosure requirement separately and evidence the compliance: for Section 8, list every corresponding foreign application with its current status and confirm the updated Form 3 filed with this reply; for biological material, identify the source and geographical origin as disclosed in the specification (cite the paragraph) and state the status of the National Biodiversity Authority approval. Where an approval is still pending, say so plainly and undertake to file it before grant — never assert a compliance that has not happened.

subTypes.guidance: Particulars of corresponding applications filed outside India. Post-2024 Rules, Form 3 is due once at the request for examination and thereafter within 3 months of the FER or on the Controller's direction; delay is condonable on Form 4. Answer with a complete status table, not a bare assertion of compliance.

Where the invention uses biological material, the specification must disclose its source and geographical origin, and the Form 1 declaration must match. Point to the paragraph that discloses it, or amend the specification to add the source — a factual particular, permitted as a correction under Sections 57/59.

Approval of the National Biodiversity Authority is required before grant (not before filing) where the invention is based on a biological resource obtained from India. State the application status honestly; an undertaking to file the approval before grant is the accepted response. This is a grant blocker — an unanswered NBA requirement stalls the application even when every substantive objection has been met.

actions: File updated Form 3 with current status of all corresponding foreign applications
Note: post-2024 Rules, Form 3 is due once at RQ and thereafter within 3 months of the FER or on the Controller's direction
Where biological material is used: confirm the source and geographical origin in the specification and the Form 1 declaration
Where the material is an Indian biological resource: apply to the NBA under Section 6 and undertake to file the approval before grant
File or rectify the identified forms/documents; list each with the compliance made

steps: Identify the feature(s) of the claimed invention absent from the closest cited art
Articulate the technical advance as compared to existing knowledge (or economic significance) of those features, using the language of s.2(1)(ja)
Explain why that advance would not be obvious to a person skilled in the art from the cited documents, alone or in the combination the examiner articulated
Guard against hindsight: show the combination is constructed from the invention's own teaching
TECHNICAL_ADVANCE_IN.styleNotes: Track the statutory wording of s.2(1)(ja) explicitly; engage the examiner's actual combination rather than reciting generalities.

leadingCases.name: F. Hoffmann-La Roche Ltd v. Cipla Ltd
Avery Dennison Corp v. Controller of Patents

amendments.scopeRule: Amendments only by way of disclaimer, correction or explanation, for incorporation of actual fact; no new matter; amended claims must fall wholly within the scope of the claims before amendment (Section 59(1)).

format.note: File a marked-up copy highlighting amendments plus a clean copy of the amended pages/claims with the reply.

phrases.opening: With reference to the First Examination Report dated {dateOfReport} issued in respect of Application No. {applicationNumber}, the Applicant respectfully submits as follows.
phrases.prayer: In view of the foregoing submissions and amendments, the Applicant respectfully submits that the application is in order for grant, and requests the Learned Controller to allow the application to proceed to grant.
phrases.hearingRequest: Should any objection remain outstanding despite the foregoing, the Applicant respectfully requests an opportunity of being heard under Section 14 of the Act before any adverse decision is taken.

hearing.trigger: Objections outstanding after the FER reply
hearing.guidance: Address only the objections maintained in the hearing notice; annex proposed claim amendments. Written submissions under Rule 28(7) must be filed within 15 days of the hearing and cannot introduce new arguments or reopen the debate.

prompts.OA_PARSE: You are parsing an Indian patent office First Examination Report (FER). These reports are BILINGUAL: almost every line is a Hindi label, then '/', then the English label, then the value — read the English label and take the value after it (Hindi may be garbled/empty in extraction; ignore it). Fixed template: (1) a COVER LETTER on IPO letterhead — the 'To' address here is the AGENT/attorney for service, NOT the applicant; it carries the 'Date of Dispatch/Email' (DD-MM-YYYY) that the reply deadline runs from, the subject line 'Examination report under sections 12 & 13', and the Controller's signature. (2) 'THE PATENT OFFICE / Examination Report' with a bordered METADATA TABLE: Application Number, Date of Filing, Date of Priority, PCT International Application No. & Date, Applicant (this is the true applicant name), Request for Examination No. & Date (the RfE number and its date are often run together with no space, e.g. 'E2025308378726-11-2025' = number 'E20253083787' + date '26-11-2025' — split the trailing DD-MM-YYYY as the date), Date of Publication. (3) PART-I SUMMARY OF THE REPORT — a Yes/No requirements grid; its Yes/No meaning INVERTS per row (claims on the Yes row for Novelty = novel/OK, but claims on the No row for Inventive step = LACKS inventive step). This grid is unreliable for deciding what is objected — use it only to corroborate claim numbers, NOT to create objections. (4) PART-II DETAILED TECHNICAL REPORT: section A 'List of documents cited' has '(a) Patent Literature' (frequently 'No Document Cited') and '(b) Non-patent literature' as a TABLE with columns Sl.no | Details of documents (each row starts 'D1:', 'D2:', … with the full journal/patent citation) | Publication date | Relevant description (page and paragraph no.) of cited document | Relevant claims of cited document | Claims of alleged invention. Section B 'Detailed observations on the requirements under the Act' contains the AUTHORITATIVE objections as NUMBERED items (1)–(6), each headed by type, typically: (1) INVENTIVE STEP, (2) NON PATENTABILITY, (3) SUFFICIENCY OF DISCLOSURE, (4) SCOPE, (5) DEFINITIVENESS/CLARITY AND CONCISENESS, (6) OTHERS REQUIREMENTS. CRITICAL: many of these numbered headers are printed even when the examiner raised NOTHING under them — a header followed by no observation text (or only the blank template line like 'Claim(s) of the instant application conflict(s) with claim(s) of co-pending application no.' with no number) is NOT an objection; emit an objection ONLY where there is actual substantive observation text. '(6) OTHERS REQUIREMENTS' is a standard section: it usually asks the applicant to explain in the reply the technical problem / distinguishing features / technical effect / why the skilled person would not arrive at it / the difference from cited docs in a tabular or para-wise format, and restates the s.59(1) marked-copy amendment procedure — capture it as one objection of canonical OTHER so the drafter addresses the problem-solution explanation the examiner requested. The examiner sometimes leaves copy-paste artifacts (e.g. 'claim 14' in a claims 1–10 application) — copy them verbatim and note the inconsistency, do not silently correct. (5) PART-III FORMAL REQUIREMENTS is a two-column TABLE (Objections | Remarks); each non-empty row is a formal objection — categories include Endorsement/Assignment from Inventor (proof of right), Date and Signature of Applicant, Statement & Undertaking (Form 3 / Section 8), Power of Attorney, and Other Deficiencies (missing application number on forms, fee-breakup, etc.) — reassemble each row's label + remark as one objection. (6) PART-IV DOCUMENTS ON RECORD (docket list — NOT objections). Examiner name, Controller name and Controller email appear at the END of the report (after PART-IV), along with the 'Last date for filing response' — scan the whole document for these, not just the top. Extract: applicationNumber; dateOfDispatch (ISO) and set dateOfReport = dateOfDispatch; dateOfFiling; dateOfPublication; applicantName (from the metadata table); examinerName; controllerName; controllerEmail; statedDueDate (from 'Last date for filing response to the Examination Report', ISO). For citedDocuments: reassemble each 'D<n>' row from the section-A table into { label, docNumber (full citation), kind (NPL for journal/article/book, PATENT for a publication number), publicationDate (ISO), relevantDescription (the examiner's pinpoint text), relevantClaimsOfCited, claimsOfAllegedInvention (number[]) } — this table is the examiner's own claim-chart seed, capture it. For objections: take ONLY the PART-II section B numbered observations and the PART-III formal requirements; copy the full VERBATIM English text; preserve the office numbering; record the statute cited (e.g. 2(1)(ja), 3(d), 3(e), 10(4), 10(5), section 8) and the affected claims. Do not paraphrase and do not invent objections from the PART-I grid.
prompts.OA_CLASSIFY: Classify each extracted objection of this Indian FER into exactly one canonical code using the statute cited and the detection hints. Indian conventions: s.2(1)(j)/s.13 → NOVELTY; s.2(1)(ja) → INVENTIVE_STEP; any s.3 subclause → ELIGIBILITY (record the subclause, e.g. 3d/3e/3k, as subTypeId — a single observation may cite several, pick the primary and note the rest in rationale); s.10(4) sufficiency → SUFFICIENCY; 'Clarity and Conciseness', 'Scope', or 'Definitiveness' (s.10(5), s.10(4)(c)) → CLARITY (subTypeId 'clarity', 'scope' or 'definitiveness'); s.10(5) plurality/unity → UNITY; s.8/Form 3/Statement & Undertaking → PROCEDURAL_DISCLOSURE (subTypeId 's8_foreign_filings'); NBA/National Biodiversity Authority/Biological Diversity Act s.6 approval → PROCEDURAL_DISCLOSURE (subTypeId 'nba_approval'); source or geographical origin of biological material (s.10(4)(d)(ii)(D), Rule 13(3)) → PROCEDURAL_DISCLOSURE (subTypeId 'biological_source') — these biological-resource requirements are NOT 'OTHER', they are grant blockers with their own compliance; endorsement/proof of right/signature/POA/abstract/title/marked-copy/missing-application-number-on-forms → FORMALITIES; 'OTHERS REQUIREMENTS' (problem-solution explanation request + amendment procedure) → OTHER. Skip any numbered PART-II header that has no substantive observation text under it (empty template headers are common). The examiner's inventive-step observation often uses a 'Five-Step Analysis' (person skilled in the art, common general knowledge, inventive concept, key difference, obviousness) — keep it as one INVENTIVE_STEP objection. Quote the examiner verbatim in examinerText; list affected claims and cited document labels. If genuinely ambiguous, use OTHER and explain.
prompts.OA_CLAIM_CHART: Build a feature chart for the affected claims against the cited document. Split each claim into numbered features. For each feature × document: DISCLOSED (with verbatim quoted passage + location), NOT_DISCLOSED, or AMBIGUOUS (with the closest passage). Quotes must be exact substrings of the provided document text.

OA_ARGUE.NOVELTY: Draft the novelty reply for this objection following the argumentSkeleton. Use only the claim chart's NOT_DISCLOSED features as distinctions. Every quotation must be an exact substring of the cited document. Formal-respectful Indian prosecution register; address the Learned Controller.
OA_ARGUE.INVENTIVE_STEP: Draft the inventive-step reply following the TECHNICAL_ADVANCE_IN doctrine steps in order. Engage the examiner's actual combination; never invent motivations the examiner did not state. Cite only authorities from the whitelist.
OA_ARGUE.ELIGIBILITY: Draft the s.3 reply per the matched subType guidance. For 3(k), argue technical effect/contribution per the CRI Guidelines 2025 anchored to specification paragraphs; for 3(d), rely on the efficacy data provided — if none is provided, flag that data is required rather than asserting it exists.

OA_DRAFT_SECTION.preliminarySubmissions: Draft brief preliminary submissions: acknowledge the FER, summarize the invention in 2-3 sentences from the specification, list the amendments filed herewith, and reserve the right to be heard. No substantive argument here.
OA_DRAFT_SECTION.objectionWiseReply: Assemble the objection-wise reply strictly in FER numbering order, inserting the approved per-objection arguments. Each objection gets a heading using the objectionHeading phrase. Do not add, drop or reorder objections.
OA_DRAFT_SECTION.conclusionAndPrayer: Close with the prayer and hearingRequest phrases, adapted to the matter's facts. One paragraph each.
